item.title: Is Your Adult Child Emotionally Bankrupting Your Other Kids?
item.description:
Parenting

Is Your Adult Child Emotionally Bankrupting Your Other Kids?

One kid gets rescued, and the other one gets used to being invisible.

Posted July 16, 2026

Key points
  • Struggle gets resources. Competence gets ignored.
  • Unspoken resentment doesn't fade. It hardens into distance.
  • Fairness isn't equal treatment. It is honest acknowledgment.

I see it every day when working with parents and families of struggling adult children. The sibling who never asked for help is quietly keeping score—and the bill comes due eventually. Every dollar, phone call, and crisis text message that makes you slip into your first responder uniform all add up in the memory of the one who does not need rescuing. Parents rarely see the pattern forming because they are in the thick of struggles that demand their immediate attention. The song "Urgent" by Foreigner comes to mind. That's because amid the emergencies of the struggling adult child, the one who is "fine" can feel lonely and isolated in trying to live up to the "low maintenance" title they have been typecast in. There is a silence that many more well-adjusted siblings suffer in. Here are three ways that silence costs.

1. Struggle Gets Resources, While Competence Is Assumed.

Children are extraordinary pattern recognizers even as adults. When one sibling struggles to provide money, compassion, and forgiveness while another's steady competence leads to the assumption that they "always have it together," you have not just created an unequal household. What I'm saying is that you have inadvertently created two narratives of what gets attention and love. One learns that falling apart works, and the other learns that needing anything can feel like a burden. I'm not saying that this negates your effort and love toward your more emotionally hardy child. But based on what many siblings have shared with me, it is crucial, as a parent, to at least consider how your hypervigilance toward the one who struggled affected the one who didn't as much.

2. Unspoken Resentment May Harden Into Distance.

The higher-functioning sibling often says little. Or, even if they express their frustrations, they learn that it will not make a difference in their parents' rescuing behaviors. So, they learn to accept that, as the "strong" brother or sister, it is not their role to complain. But resentment that is not spoken does not evaporate. In fact, it can lead to distance. I have seen that, years later, parents are baffled by who is short on the phone, hard to reach, or no longer so available to meet on holidays. This may feel sudden, but in reality, it isn't. It was building for years, as the families' almost entire emotional and financial bandwidth was redirected to someone else indefinitely, without truly naming it out loud.

This dynamic is related to what I write about in my book You've Ruined My Life, Now You Owe Me! The impact of struggling adult children often shines a spotlight on beleaguered parents. Yet the siblings often suffer the immense collateral impacts as well. This sadly happens in many cases where the parents did not intend it. It's like the whole family ecosystem of intended attention has been reshaped by repeated need for indefinite urgent attention to the struggling adult child.

3. Fairness Is Not Equal Treatment. It Is Honest Acknowledgment.

You are not a failure as a parent if anything I have written above sounds familiar. No one can expect you to perfectly appropriate a fund of attention to children with starkly different levels of functioning and apparent consequent needs. But if there is any sense of failure, it may be in avoiding acknowledging to your more capable child or children the impact they have had to absorb, what they may have had to sacrifice. Essentially, what were the costs they endured for not needing to be saved? Based on what I have seen in the parent coaching trenches, that single acknowledgment, said plainly without long explanation or defensiveness, does more to repair relationships than any after-the-fact acts of fairness ever could.

The Takeaway

If you have more than one adult child and only one keeps you up at night, ask yourself honestly what they learned about what it takes to feel they matter in your family. Their silence is not peace; it is valuable data.

item.title: A Detour on the Path to Happiness
item.description:
Happiness

A Detour on the Path to Happiness

Why pursuing happiness may not be a straight shot for some.

Posted July 16, 2026

Key points
  • Cultivating friendships, the number one ingredient of happiness, can be out of reach for some people.
  • Making friends and creating social ties is a learned skill.
  • Most children learn loving closeness from their experience of it with their parents and siblings. Some don't.
  • You may need skill building to do what comes naturally to others.

Consciously pursuing happiness is a wonderful idea. I love that we now have a science of happiness and that “positive psychology” courses taught on the subject turn out to be the most popular ones ever offered at top universities like Yale. How could it not be good to know, for example, that cultivating friendships is number one on positive psychology’s list of happiness ingredients? Better than dedicatedly pursuing money or success without considering alternatives. But maybe we should pause a moment to take note that the path to happiness may be blocked for some people? Cultivating friendships—like pursuing any of the activities that lead to happiness—is predicated on being able to. What happens if you’re not? In my experience, a lot of people arrive at young adulthood emotionally hampered, though they might not realize it. I didn’t, despite arriving at college with some heavy fears and pain. Not to speak of a defense system I developed to stay as far from those feelings as possible, no matter the sacrifice. Without awareness and remedial help, that friendship goal—even if I could have formulated it—was out of reach for me.

Connecting with others may be a natural and fundamental human need, but it’s also a learned skill. Good enough parents not only model happiness-producing friendships, but their own close, loving connection with their child is, in itself, the practice of closeness for all involved, which imprints itself on the child. Unfortunately, not everyone has those parents. Some can be too bogged down in their own problems or their own growing up to bond deeply with their children; alcohol, anger, or depression might have stood in the way. My friend Kathy’s mother had a martini in hand by the time we got home from school in 7th grade. Michael’s father threw a television at him once. Could have killed him, he said. My mother wasn’t that bad. But as anyone who's read pretty much any of my writing knows, my mother, having suffered one trauma too many, was distant, rarely engaged in my world or interested in who I was. She herself had only one or two good friends, neither of whom she replaced after they died young. If she modeled any social behavior, it was self-containment and self-sufficiency. I never felt the connection to her that I unconsciously longed for and got a taste of with a loving brother and a couple of cousins.

As much as I valued the social connections that happiness scientists advise, by college, I was too socially isolated and insecure to make them. Many people do make lasting friends in high school, or even before, but by high school, I went from my classes to my after-school job and home to homework and bed. No boyfriends. Scarcely any friends. I just thought of myself as serious and studious instead of realizing I was avoiding what I feared I’d fail at. Or just feared. In college, I befriended the two loner girls on my hall who were as socially awkward as I was. On weekends, we might get together to listen to records while other girls were dressing up for parties and dates. It never occurred to us to join groups or clubs. Expand our social lives.

The problem is this: If, for protective reasons, your unconscious has steered you away from what’s painful or frightening, in my case, social ties, you lack social experience and expectations of success. The more time you spend alone in your own fantasy world, the more unapproachable and alien you may appear to others, as I found out from Michael, a classmate who became my friend once I did find my social way.

Like most young people who feel like outsiders, I didn’t understand what was going on with me. I just thought if I buttoned up and did my work, I could ignore a feeling of lostness, or maybe emptiness, that could suffuse me with an ache that, for a while, I'd blunt with weed. Back then, though, I was at its mercy. Now I understand that by not pursuing friendships, I unconsciously avoided being flooded with that very longing for more connection that I’d felt throughout my childhood. And the pain of not getting it.

What helped was falling apart. By the end of my second year, I’d begun to break down in tears every few days, mostly in my room but sometimes even in public. I couldn’t control it. But I also couldn’t afford a nervous breakdown. Literally. I thought that if I didn’t get a graduate degree ASAP, I wouldn’t be able to pay back my loans and support myself. That’s when I went for help. Of course, I didn’t tell anyone and didn’t know how to find a therapist on my own. The random psychiatrist I stumbled on was a disaster. When I finally dared to tell my housemate—and probably it just slipped out when I wasn’t keeping to myself—she surprised me by lighting up and saying that she saw a wonderful one herself and recommended his office mate, who turned out to be warm and welcoming. Once Dr. Robertson recognized my isolation, he made remedying it seem so simple. Like a coach would. Like the parent I’d really never had to help me find my social place, he was interested in what I had to say and made me feel charming. He laughed at my jokes and worked with whatever social interaction I reported—a boy who gave me a lift in the rain, a girl who helped me with my paper. He cheered me when I joined a political action group and, taking a wild leap about a year later, tried out for a play, a comedy no less, and got a part.

It sounds easy, but for some people, it’s not easy to 1) realize you might not be able to do something that should come naturally, 2) look deeply into the reasons why and face the hurts you’ve carried with you into young adulthood, and 3) realize that you may want to get help.
